questions.question: Why does `function f(v: string | number) { return v.toUpperCase(); }` fail to compile?
options: toUpperCase does not exist on strings
Unions cannot be used as parameter types
Only members shared by every type in the union can be used, and number has no toUpperCase
questions.explanation: Without narrowing, TypeScript only allows operations valid for all members of the union.

questions.question: With strict mode, `function find(): string | null` is called as `const n = find(); n.length;`. What happens?
options: It compiles; null checks are only done at runtime
It compiles but n is typed any
questions.explanation: With strict null checks, null must be handled before accessing properties, for example with a check or optional chaining.

questions.question: What makes a union of object types a discriminated union?
options: Every member is declared with interface
Every member has exactly the same set of properties
Every member has a shared property with a distinct literal value, such as method: "upi" or method: "card"
The union has exactly two members
questions.explanation: A shared literal-typed property (the discriminant) lets TypeScript narrow to the right member when you check its value.
